content.thinking:
I'm checking the discrepancy between when the flag was actually toggled (recorded at 12:49:45 by admin per P1) versus when errors actually began at 12:44 — the candidate claims the toggle happened at 12:44, but the log record shows it came after onset, which matters for the timeline.

Looking further, the mitigation turned off at 12:49:54 doesn't seem to have fixed things — the service isn't back at baseline (M1 refuted), and ZeroDivisionError occurrences in spend_summary.py:47 continue through 13:00 even after the flag was supposedly disabled. Since rollback isn't possible given there's no earlier revision, and errors persisted post-mitigation, I think the honest conclusion is that the flag toggle timing doesn't cleanly establish it as the trigger, and the actual root cause behind the division-by-zero remains unresolved — I should be upfront that the incident is still unresolved rather than forcing a tidy narrative.

Other contributing factors: lack of flag-change tie to error correlation, inconsistent timestamps between flag audit logs and evaluation logs, no guarded rollout, and no test coverage for the zero-division case; Argus's mitigation attempt appears to have been refuted after a long wait. I should draft action items—fixing the division-by-zero with a guard and test, staged flag rollout, retaining previous revisions for rollback, reconciling the timestamp discrepancy, and alerting on flag-change correlation—numbering them as AI-1 and onward.

I'll avoid citing specific figures like durations or exact timestamps, keeping references general (such as "the spend-summary module" rather than a specific line number) while still using placeholders like {duration} and {began} where needed.

action_items.item: Guard the divisor at the division in the spend-summary code, with a defined fallback for the zero case. Add a regression test for that input, and find out what input produces the zero.
Put monthly-spend-feature and similar flags behind a percentage rollout with an automatic turn-off when the error rate on the affected pages rises.
Keep at least one previous deployable revision for io-shop, and check before an incident that rollback works.

Find why the flag audit event is stamped after the first on evaluations and errors. Make flag audit events and evaluation logs use one reliable clock so responders can tell whether a flag change preceded the onset.
Make Argus compare the error rate shortly after a mitigation and move to the next candidate sooner when the error rate is not falling, instead of waiting out the full window.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw account-page requests fail. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}, starting at {began}. It had still not recovered at the last minute of metrics read.

The failing requests were raising ZeroDivisionError in the spend-summary code (spend_summary.py). These errors began at the onset and were still being logged at the end of the window. The ClientDisconnected errors were a small background level and did not explain the rise.

The spend-summary path was being taken more and more as monthly-spend-feature evaluated on. Evaluations were split between off and on at the onset and were mostly on soon after. An admin's flag change to on is the only production change in the record, and no deploy was read.

Switching the flag off did not bring the service back, and the on evaluations and division errors were still logged afterwards. The flag therefore cannot be shown to be the whole cause. The flag change is also stamped after the onset, which the record cannot reconcile with the evaluation logs. A rollback was impossible because the deployment had no earlier revision. The record stops here, and the reason the divisor is zero is unknown.

contributing_factors.factor: The spend-summary code divides without guarding against a zero divisor, and no test covered that input before the flag exposed the path to users.
The flag was changed for all traffic at once with no staged rollout or automatic error-rate guard, so a faulty path reached shoppers immediately.
The deployment had no earlier revision, so rollback, the second mitigation, was impossible and the incident had to be escalated.
Flag-change timestamps and flag-evaluation logs disagree about when the flag went on. This blurred whether the flag caused the onset and made the first mitigation a guess.
Argus waited out the whole verification window on a mitigation that was not working before it tried anything else. Nothing flagged that errors were continuing after the flag went off.

input.executive_summary: Shoppers using the shop's account pages got errors. The failure rate rose from {errors_before} to an average of {errors_while_broken} and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. It had not recovered when the metrics reading stopped, so the outage lasted at least {duration}. Every impact figure is a lower bound. The errors came from a calculation in the monthly-spend-summary code that divides by zero. That code was released behind a feature flag. Argus switched the flag off, but errors continued, so it put the flag back. It then tried to roll the service back to its previous version, but no earlier version existed. Argus escalated to people after {held}. The service was not shown to be recovered, and the underlying fault is not yet fixed.

got_lucky: The failure was a clear ZeroDivisionError with a code location in the logs, so people taking over know where to look.
went_well: Argus read the metrics, logs, changes and flag history in a few seconds and acted on a leading candidate within moments of the alert.
The flag revert was undone when it did not help, so Argus left no extra change behind.
Argus escalated clearly when rollback was impossible.
went_wrong: The first mitigation did not recover the service, and the long wait before judging it delayed the next attempt.
The second mitigation, rollback, could not run because there was no earlier revision.
The trigger was never confirmed, and the service was not shown to have recovered when the incident was handed off.
The flag change was stamped after the onset, which weakened the evidence for the leading candidate.

input.root_cause: Account-page requests hit an unguarded division by zero in the spend-summary code (spend_summary.py). The errors began at the onset and carried on after the monthly-spend-feature flag was switched off. The record does not show what input makes the divisor zero. It also does not show that the flag was the trigger, because the flag change is logged after the onset.
